subject: chopperMotorbike
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: custom chopper motorbike.
Style: Overwatch.
reasoning:
I'm planning a single TypeScript module for an Overwatch-style chopper motorbike, aiming for a substantial but realistic length while making sure I use the SDK API correctly since I won't be able to test it, with a default export function returning b.root and an exported meta.

For the Overwatch aesthetic, I'm leaning toward bold, clean cel-ish shading with an orange/white/charcoal/cyan palette and glowing accents — probably combining the glow kit for lights with custom paint functions for lighting on the body panels, keeping the toolset simple to avoid errors. I'm also sketching the chopper's form: a long raked front fork as the defining silhouette element.

I'm working out realistic proportions — roughly 2.6m long, 1.2m to the handlebars, a big 21" front wheel and smaller 16" rear, with a long wheelbase and springer fork at a steep rake angle, keeping the bike riderless since the brief's subject is the vehicle itself and no ground plane is needed. Now I'm thinking through the joint structure, considering how the wheels should rotate and what roles to assign them within the available skeleton vocabulary.

Mapping out the skeleton: a root frame joint at the center of mass, a steering joint at the head tube angled along the raked fork, and separate front/rear axle joints, calculating the fork's forward-and-down geometry to position the front axle relative to the head tube at roughly a 46° angle from vertical.

I'm placing the front and rear wheel joints with axles oriented along X so they spin naturally, setting the wheelbase around 2.5-2.7m between front and rear axles, and skipping a rider in favor of a sissy bar detail.

Now I'm designing the fuel tank as a teardrop loft shape using catmull stations that narrow at front and tail and widen in the middle, sitting atop a stick-style frame with down tubes and backbone. For the overall look I'm going for an Overwatch-inspired aesthetic: bold white body panels with orange and cyan accents, a dark charcoal frame, chrome steel parts, and a glowing cyan headlight.

I'm figuring out how to decal the tank with a stylized emblem (a chevron stripe design) using an SVG texture placed on the loft surface via b.decal, then checking the b.loft signature for defining stations with position, width, height, color, and bone attachment to the frame. Next I'm sketching the front springer fork with paired tubes running from the head tube to the front axle, plus a triple tree component.

Now I'm working out the geometry for the fork legs and steering joint, positioning them symmetrically around the axle and defining the steering joint's orientation so the fork and handlebars pivot correctly as children. I'm also planning ape-hanger handlebars rising up and back from the triple tree to grip points, using a swept path with capsule-style grips, all parented to the steering bone.

For the colour palette I'm settling on an Overwatch-inspired scheme: white body, orange accent, cyan glow, navy frame, gunmetal and chrome details, black tyres with pale rims and orange hubs. I'm deciding to lean on the toon kit's cel shading for that painterly, stylized look across the body and frame, paired with the glow kit for the headlight and light strips, while keeping wheel treads simple with chunky cylinder segments rather than adding extra texture kits.

I'm working out how to place tread blocks around the tyre using a ring arrangement tied to the wheel's joint axis so the blocks spin correctly with the wheel, oriented outward from the tyre's circumference.

Now I'm figuring out how to attach the wheel's cylinder geometry to the axle joint, aligning its orientation so the cylinder's default Y-axis matches the joint's facing direction along X.

For the actual wheel shape, I'm leaning toward a torus for the tyre since it gives that chunky, rounded stylized look fitting the chopper aesthetic, aiming its default Z-axis along X to match the axle. I'm planning a rim disc inside it, and considering tread blocks only on the fatter rear tyre while keeping the front tyre narrow and plain.

Now I'm working through the math to get wheel radii and axle heights so both tyres sit flush on the ground, settling on front torus R=0.28/tube=0.045 and rear R=0.25/tube=0.08 for an outer radius around 0.325-0.33 each, with axle centers set to match. I'm placing the front axle further forward in z and the rear axle back, then checking that the raked fork length from the head tube to the front axle comes out to roughly a meter, which feels right for a long chopper-style fork.

I'm recalculating total vehicle length by accounting for tyre width extending along z since the torus tubes run along x, and trimming the axle positions down to about a 2.25m wheelbase to keep the overall length closer to a realistic 2.6-2.9m chopper proportions rather than the overly stretched 3.25m I got initially.

Now I'm designing the engine block as a chunky V-twin shape sitting roughly centered below the frame — a dark gunmetal box with two angled cylinder heads positioned to form the classic V silhouette when viewed from the side.

I'm also sketching out the frame geometry: a downtube running from the head to the engine, a backbone sweeping from head through the tank to the seat post, rear struts connecting to the axle, and a swingarm pair flanking the rear wheel.

Now I'm setting up the joint hierarchy -- a frame root joint, a steer joint for the fork, and wheel joints for front and rear -- and thinking through which roles to assign, settling on "spine" for the frame and "hinge" for the steer and wheels to keep things simple rather than overengineering the rig.

For the actual body panels, I'm planning to paint the tank using a custom paint function layered under cel shading, applying a white base with an orange stripe band based on position and surface normal. I'm leaning toward an Overwatch-inspired palette -- clean white, bold orange accents, and navy trim -- to get that hard-edged heroic look, defining the hex colors I'll use throughout the model.

Building the skeleton hierarchy...

Still defining swingarm and fork geometry...

For the front fender, I'm working out a chopper-style stretched fender using an arc sweep around the front wheel's axle, figuring out rotation direction and angle range so it covers the tire from top down toward the front.

Working out the fender sweep dimensions, using a flat radius profile (width sideways, thin radially) so it looks like a sheet rather than a tube, and deciding it should attach to the steer bone but stay non-spinning since it should follow steering but not wheel rotation.

I'm also checking geometry to make sure the fender arc doesn't collide with the fork legs — the legs sit at roughly -42° from the axle while the fender spans -25° to 85°, so they shouldn't overlap. Moving on to the tank next, planning to loft it from stations and attach it to the frame bone at y=0.

Now I'm setting up the tank's cross-section stations along its length, placing them around y≈0.9-0.97 so they sit above the backbone and taper from a narrow front near the head tube to a wider mid-section and back down toward the seat. I'm defining a tank paint pattern — white body with orange flame stripes on the sides keyed to surface normal and position along the loft's parametric coordinate.

Next I'm sketching the seat as a separate loft: a low, long chopper-style seat tapering from front to rear with a slight rise at the back, positioned over the rear rails and tank in deep navy leather.

I need to adjust the tank's rear station so it ends earlier and taper the seat stations so the two don't overlap, placing the seat behind the tank from roughly z -0.3 to -0.7. Then I'll start building the rear fender as an arc around the rear axle for a bobbed/stretched chopper look.

For the engine, I'm planning a V-twin using two angled cylinders for the heads/barrels mounted on the frame, and considering whether to add fins or just keep it simple with chrome coloring on the cylinders.

I'm checking the crankcase box dimensions and position against the downtube to make sure it fits, then verifying the splayed cylinders' top positions don't collide with the fuel tank's bottom edge at various z-stations — it looks like there's just enough clearance.

For the rear cylinder I'm mirroring the same splay angle downward in z, keeping both V-twin cylinders thick and chunky to match the chopper aesthetic. Now I'm plotting a curved exhaust pipe path sweeping from the front cylinder down along the right side toward the rear, using a chrome finish with a darker tip band near the end.

I'm double-checking the exhaust pipe's clearance against the rear fender radius, nudging the endpoint slightly so it just grazes the fender without clipping through it. Now I'm positioning a cyan Overwatch-style headlight sphere on a bracket just ahead of the fork crown, checking its placement against the fork legs so it sits forward without overlapping them.

For the headlight I'm using the glow kit to make the sphere self-illuminated, and adding a chrome torus bezel ring around it -- making sure to set its orientation axis to "z" so the ring faces forward correctly rather than lying flat in the wrong plane.

Now I'm laying out ape hanger handlebars using a catmull curve that sweeps up from the grips near the triple tree, rising and curving back toward center before mirroring symmetrically to the other grip, all rendered as a thin chrome rod on the steer bone.

Now I'm positioning the handlebar center above the triple tree clamp, then moving on to the seat details and sketching out the sissy bar geometry curving up behind the seat from the frame's rear point.

For the rear wheel, I'm planning the torus tire with tread blocks attached around its radius, working out how to orient each box so its height aligns radially outward from the tire surface while its width spans the tire's axial direction.

Actually simplifying the tread approach - I'll use a torus with few radial segments for a chunky faceted profile rather than separate tread blocks, which reads better at the stylized scale. For the rim, I'm going with a bold disc hub with orange coloring plus spokes radiating out to the rim, giving it that chopper-wheel look rather than a plain cylinder.

For spokes, I'm thinking rods connecting hub to rim using rod(a, b, radius, color, opts) with a hub-center point and rim items from a ring at radius 0.19, going radial rather than tangential for simplicity, even though that's less realistic than real wagon-wheel spokes. I could use two concentric rings — one small at radius 0.06 near the hub, one larger at 0.19 at the rim — and connect matching angles with rods.

Actually, offsetting the connection by one index between inner and outer rings would give tangential-style spokes, which looks more natural. I'm reconsidering whether a solid disc at x=0 would clash with spokes occupying the same plane, and thinking it's cleaner to skip the disc entirely and just use spokes plus a hub and a tire/rim torus.

I'm leaning toward a stylized asymmetry: the rear wheel as a bold orange solid disc with a chrome rim torus, while the front wheel keeps a lighter 12-spoke chrome look for contrast, with the tire torus sized so the disc tucks inside it. I'm also sketching out decal ideas for the tank — a bold emblem with chevron stripes in orange against white, maybe with a cyan accent, to apply as a texture decal on both tank sides.

Now I'm working out decal placement and orientation so the emblem sits correctly on each flank, considering whether to mirror the decal for the opposite side so it doesn't read backwards.

Since I'm using a symmetrical shield/chevron emblem, mirroring won't actually matter visually, which simplifies things. I'm also sketching out the emblem's SVG design and considering adding a cyan underglow strip along the fender for an Overwatch-style neon accent.

I'm planning additional glow details: a cyan accent stripe on the front fender, a small orange ember glow sphere at the exhaust tip, and a red tail light glow positioned near the rear fender, working out its coordinates based on the fender's curve.

Settling on tail light position around (0, 0.43, -1.33), tucked behind the fender lip using an arc calculation. I'm deciding to skip the air cleaner and oil tank details since they'd be hidden under the tank, and moving on to adding small chrome foot peg boxes near the frame at roughly (±0.2, 0.36, 0.05).

Now I'm sketching the drivetrain: forward foot pegs with a mirror, then a rear sprocket cylinder at the axle and a chain rod connecting it to the engine's front sprocket, while checking that the sprocket sits outside the tire width so it doesn't clip through the wheel.

I'm worried the sprocket position collides with the exhaust pipe, so I decide to shift the exhaust slightly outward and simplify by dropping the explicit chain geometry, instead attaching a small chrome sprocket cylinder to the rear wheel bone so it spins naturally. Then I'm confirming the joint hierarchy -- the "steer" joint parents all the front-end parts, and the root "frame" joint has no parent -- before estimating the module will land around 400-500 lines total, prioritizing quality over hitting a strict length target.

I'm also double-checking which toon-shading helpers to pull in for cel-shaded materials and ink accents on the tires, then verifying the builder API signatures for joints, lofts, sweeps, rods, parts, and rings against how they're used in the reference example to make sure my calls match the expected parameters.

Setting up color palette constants...

Working out the stripe placement using normal and position checks for the orange side band and navy top panel, then confirming cel shading nests properly with paint functions so lit colors resolve correctly for shadow calculation. I'm also adding a glowing cyan sphere for the headlight and starting on an SVG emblem decal for the tank's texture.

Writing SVG decal code...

Now I'm defining the axle and head position constants as simple number arrays, checking that these literal tuples work fine as point inputs for the geometry builder.

I'm sketching out helper functions for mirroring points and placing wheel joints, favoring plain tuple-returning functions over `as const` to keep typing simple, then starting the module imports for the three.js builder, toon shading kit, and glow effects before setting up the chopper's metadata.

Now I'm building out the skeleton joints for the frame, steering hinge, and front/rear wheels, defining their parent relationships, positions, and orientation directions to establish the bike's basic structure.

Still writing frame geometry...

I'm adding the lower frame rail, swingarm rods, and seat stays connecting the backbone to the rear axle, then starting the engine crankcase geometry with a steel-colored box.

Now I'm positioning the V-twin cylinders, calculating their centers and angled directions so front and rear cylinders splay outward from the crankcase, then adding chrome heads on top and considering fin details for the cylinder bodies.

I'm building the fuel tank with a loft across four stations, defining a paint function that colors the top navy, a mid stripe orange, and the rest white, then checking that the tank's shape properly clears the backbone frame at each z-station without clipping.

I realize the mid tank station makes the tank too tall and could collide with the handlebars, so I'm lowering its height and rechecking the stripe position and front station clearance against the head tube. Now I'm moving to the seat, lofting it from a station near the tank's rear end and noticing it slightly overlaps the tank there, so I'll need to adjust the widths to avoid interpenetration.

Adjusting the sissy bar base to connect with the rear frame, then adding a chrome pad sphere at the top. I'm now working through the front end triple tree and head tube geometry, figuring out how to orient the head tube cylinder correctly relative to the steer bone's fork angle versus world axes.

Writing fork leg rods...

Finishing risers at that endpoint, then adding dark-colored grip rods extending outward from the bar ends. For the headlight, I'm placing a glowing sphere lamp on the steering bone near the triple tree front, adjusting its depth so it sits flush against the fork plate rather than floating or clipping through it.

I'm adding a small steel bracket rod to bridge the gap between the triple tree and lamp, then wrapping a chrome torus bezel around the lamp's equator for a ring-light look, possibly with a cyan accent for style. Now I'm shifting to the front fender, working out an arc path that follows the wheel's curvature using a helper function to compute points along the wheel radius at given angles.

Verifying the rotation math...

Setting up the fender arc geometry, then sweeping an elliptical cross-section tube along that path in white to match the Overwatch-style color scheme.

Adding a thin glowing cyan ribbon along the fender's outer edge for the accent stripe, then defining the rear fender arc and sweep with similar parameters, bone-linked to the frame.

I'm settling on orange for the rear fender and white for the front to keep bold contrast. Then I'm building the rear tyre torus geometry aimed outward along X with bone wheelR, followed by the rear brake disc as a cylinder sized to fit inside the tyre.

Still working through the tread block placement around the wheel ring, checking that the box geometry pokes out slightly from the torus surface for a visible tread effect.

Checking the stick embed parameters and spacing math, then moving on to building the front tyre torus...

Now I'm working out the front wheel's hub and spokes: placing twelve rods between an inner ring at radius 0.06 and an outer ring at radius 0.2, both bound to the front wheel bone, with a chrome cylindrical hub sitting inside the spoke ring. I'm applying similar hub logic to the rear wheel, which uses a solid disc instead of spokes, and now I'm thinking through the rear axle and swingarm placement.

Then I'm placing the rear sprocket as a small chrome cylinder near the rear wheel bone, adding forward-control footpegs as steel boxes connected to the frame by angled rods, and finally sketching out a sweeping exhaust pipe that curves from the engine area down and back up along the bike's side, using a catmull spline path with chrome coloring and banded shading toward the tip.

I'm checking that the exhaust pipe's path doesn't clash with the crankcase or rear tire by nudging its x-offset further outward, past the rear sprocket and footpeg positions, so it reads as running clearly alongside the engine rather than through it.

I'm placing the pipe's bend points down toward the rear, verifying the tip sits near the fender without actually intersecting it, then adding a small glowing orange sphere at the exhaust tip for that heated-metal effect. Then I shift to positioning the swingarm rods, adjusting their x-offset slightly wider than the tire edge so the pivot-to-axle connection reads cleanly without overlapping the sprocket.

Next I'm placing seat stays connecting the backbone to the rear axle area, confirming the clearance works, then adding a small chrome cylinder gas cap on top of the tank, nudging its height up slightly so it sits flush on the tank's curved top surface. Finally I start adding emblem decals on both tank sides, positioning them symmetrically and checking the tank's width at that z-station to make sure the decal size fits within the panel.

Verifying the emblem placement against the tank's taper and orange stripe to confirm the decal lands correctly on the surface without needing a separate mirrored version, and noting the overall part count is manageable before shifting into defining the chrome paint shader based on surface normals.

Now I'm checking that painted rods and cel-colored parts correctly share material sheets since glow effects won't apply to painted ones, and confirming the loft stations for the tank and grip colors are typed and set up properly.

I'm adding cyan glow accents for an Overwatch-inspired look — a lamp, fender line, exhaust ember, and a small red glow box positioned at the rear fender for the tail light. I'm settling on bold color blocking overall: white body, navy frame, orange accents, cyan glow, and finalizing the root export along with a meta object naming the build "Chopper."

Now I'm double-checking the builder API signatures — sweep, rod, ring, stick, and joint calls — to make sure parent/child bone references, aim targets, and point inputs like the front axle and head joint are all wired correctly for the steering fork and wheel placement.

Checking overall proportions next: total bike length comes out around 2.9m with front and rear wheel extents, handlebar height around 1.4m fitting chopper style, and handlebar width at ±0.45m for the ape-hanger look — all reasonable.

Writing helper code to compute a point on a wheel's circle given angle and radius...

I'm also sanity-checking the fender arc geometry — making sure the trim tube radius sits correctly atop the fender's cross-section so it doesn't clip through, and double-checking which axis the sweep's rx/ry correspond to (sideways vs radial normal) to avoid a misaligned trim line.

Confirming the rear fender's start angle and sweep direction match the right-hand rule around the X axis, then sketching the glowing cyan trim as a thin swept tube bound to the steering bone.

Now I'm positioning the V-twin engine cylinders angled outward from the frame on either side of centerline, computing where the cylinder caps and heads should sit based on the tilted direction vectors.

Setting up a dark steel crankcase box at the frame's base to anchor the engine, then finalizing color palette choices for the engine and chrome details before starting the full code with imports for the geometry builder and color utilities.

I'm defining the chopper's metadata, color palette (white, orange, navy, cyan, red glow), and key axle/frame positions, then writing paint functions that shade the chrome and tank surfaces based on surface normals.

Building skeleton joints...

Adding engine cylinder heads and fin details...

Now I'm shaping the fuel tank with a loft profile and positioning the gas cap, then starting on the head tube and triple tree geometry for the steering assembly.

I'm placing the fork legs connecting the triple tree to the front axle, then building the handlebars using a swept catmull-rom curve with chrome rods for risers and rubber grips at the ends.

Now I'm adding a glowing cyan headlight sphere mounted on the steer bone, with a steel bracket and torus bezel framing it.

I'm now realizing the fender sweep's cross-section needs to be a function returning an elliptical radius pair like `() => [0.07, 0.012]` rather than a linear taper array, since `[r0, r1]` means something different in the sweep API—I need to fix this for both the front fender and the glowing trim arc.

Working through the rear fender sweep, the front wheel's torus tire and hub geometry, and the spoke rods connecting the hub ring to the rim ring, checking whether the ring item types are compatible with the rod bone parameter.

Writing rear wheel geometry...

Checking that the disc is visible through the tire's inner circle from the side, that reads fine visually. Now I'm building the seat with a loft shape tapering from the tank area back toward the sissy bar, but I'm noticing the backbone frame member might poke through the seat geometry near the rear since their vertical spans overlap around z -0.3 — I should nudge the seat up or thin the backbone there to avoid clipping.

I'm also considering adding a stitched accent color to the seat, maybe an orange rear band using a paint function resolved through the cel shading pass, then building the sissy bar with a swept catmull curve plus a crossbar rod in chrome. Now I'm starting the exhaust pipe geometry with a catmull curve.

Writing pipe geometry...

Then I'm adding a glowing orange ember sphere at the pipe's tip to cap it, before moving on to the foot pegs and controls, sketching box geometry for each side.

I'm placing the tail light as a glowing red box positioned on the rear fender using the wheel arc helper, checking the math to confirm it sits just outside the fender surface. Then I move to the gas cap (a small chrome cylinder on top of the tank) and start setting up emblem decals on each side of the tank surface.

I'm now double-checking ground clearance across the whole bike: front and rear tires both bottom out exactly at y=0, the exhaust pipe clears by a small margin, and the lower frame rail and pegs sit comfortably above the floor. I'm also considering whether the tire torus geometry's limited radial segments actually produces a vertex at the true bottom point or just near it.

Checking the torus parameters confirms the front wheel's 16 tubular segments align a vertex exactly at the bottom, while the rear wheel needs matching segment counts (switching to 16 as well) to keep the lowest point close to the ground. Tread block spacing of 16 around the rear tire circumference also checks out, and the glowing parts (headlight, trim, ember, tail) all seem accounted for.

I'm verifying joint counts (frame, steer, wheelF, wheelR = 4), confirming paint definitions like cWhite, cOrange, cNavy, and cTyre are properly derived via cel() for lit/shadow shading, and double-checking that imports like arc, catmull, createBuilder, paint, and svg are correctly exported from the SDK root. I'm also making sure there's no naming collision between my local "frame" variable and any imported function, and verifying type correctness for direction arrays, decal surfaces, and wheel callback return types.

Now I'm checking for unused variables that might trip up lint/typecheck, making sure tank, seat, pipe, bars, trim, and frontFender are all actually referenced. I'm also considering adding richer detail to hit the target line count—fork shrouds, fender brackets, tank knee pads, and seat studs—to make the model feel more complete without unnecessary bloat.

Writing bolt/rivet code...

I'm sketching out additional details to round out the model: fork gaiters, maybe a rear number plate (though that risks duplicating the emblem, so I'll skip it), and orange-banded fork shrouds using sweep paths with color bands along the tube. I'm settling on keeping the design restrained rather than over-adding.

I'm reviewing SDK signatures for loft, sweep, arc, and catmull to make sure I'm using them correctly, confirming that Part objects expose a mesh property, and double-checking the emblem SVG markup before finalizing.

Defining color palette and helper types...

Writing joint/skeleton setup...

Writing frame sweep code...

Writing engine cylinder loop...

I'm placing the cooling fins and cylinder heads along each cylinder's axis using an interpolation helper, calculating fin positions and head caps so they land within the 0 to 0.3 length range of each piston barrel, and verifying the resulting world-space position for the front cylinder head lines up with where I expect the tank area to begin.

I'm checking that the engine's cylinder heads tuck slightly under the tank and seat regions, accepting minor overlap since it'll just read visually as parts nestled together rather than looking broken.

Writing tank decal and rivet code...

I'm verifying the ray directions for placing rivets on each side of the tank flank, confirming the origin and direction signs correctly hit the +X and -X sides, and double-checking that decal and stick calls accept the types being passed. I'm also reviewing wheel hub, rim, and disc construction, tweaking the torus segment count for a smoother cross-section, and confirming paint/cel color helper signatures are compatible before wrapping up and outputting the final code block with minimal surrounding text.
